Who Jesus was for us? Start where it will surprise you: on Christ himself we said what our opponents said. Word for word, creed for creed. Nobody in Africa called the other side heretics, because nobody could. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

But if you ask what of him we kept nearest, we can tell you, because the answer shows up wherever our own people are allowed to speak at length. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. And a bishop writing to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us — it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian — our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands — whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

I cannot tell you what to do with that. Not because I am withholding an answer, but because none of us left one. What a believer felt who wavered, who feared, or who quietly drifted back to the rival church — none of that is in our own words anywhere. A record kept by our enemies does not preserve those feelings. What it preserves is vindication and defiant joy, and it preserves them because they sit in the martyr texts nobody edited.

What I can tell you is how belief was made among us, not how it was kept when it faltered. A person came to believe by walking to one font and not the other one. That sounds small until you stand in an African town and see that there are two of everything — two bishops, two basilicas, two men who will say the words over you. Coming to believe was not a private settling of the mind among us. It was a public act with a date on it, and everyone in the street knew which way you had walked.

Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

Now, if you are pressing me on how we understood the relation between Father, Son and Spirit — how the three are one, what belongs to each, how the begetting works — we did not argue that, and we left no teaching on it. What did we argue about among ourselves? Two things, and we lost badly at both. The first was a broken election among our own bishops. The second was a book. Tyconius, a layman of ours, argued from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our own bishop at Carthage saw exactly where that led, wrote to him, and told him never to preach it again. Tyconius did not recant and did not leave. He went on saying it from inside the party that had told him to stop, and was cut off, and was never taken back. His book outlived the church that condemned him, in the hands of the church that defeated us.

So: we believed about God what our opponents believed about God. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead. The one question we did argue, and argued well, was whose hand may give what the church gives. What we look to is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. That is the whole strange shape of us in one clause: the interior life we were most careful about was never the believer's own. It was the interior life of the man holding the water.

We held the same creed the church we fought held, word for word. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we said it in the same Latin they said it in, and nobody in Africa called the other side heretics, because nobody could. The quarrel was never about who God is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

But if you ask what of God we kept nearest, we can show you where it appears when our own people speak at length. At Carthage, before an imperial judge who courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop thanked him and refused: We do not blush, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit - and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the God we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

Beyond that one glimpse - what we actually said about the Trinity, about God's attributes, about his nature as such - we did not write it down. We were not a teaching movement in that sense. What we argued, and argued fiercely, was one question: whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and built no school of theology beyond it. I would rather tell you we do not know what else we thought about God than hand you a confident account nobody here ever gave.

A council of bishops decided, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself. 

You can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive - the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days. Read that one and you will see how we thought a case ought to be handled: our own bishop of Caesarea would not let the court touch the merits until it had settled, in order, the day, the mandate, the persons, and only then the cause. First find out who is in the room and by what warrant. Then argue.

But we have to tell you where that actually broke down. We produced one man who could think, and we silenced him. Tyconius argued from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our own bishop told him never to preach it again. He did not recant and he did not leave, and we cut him off, and his book outlived us in the hands of the church that beat us.

So the honest answer is this: councils decided, when the question was who held office. They failed to decide when the question was what Scripture actually taught.

What survives is the record of those who held firm: the martyrs, the councils, the bishops who argued the case. We would want that examination, and we would not pretend everything we say stands the same way.

What would survive best is what can be checked without a hostile hand holding the pen. The two-party structure is beyond dispute: an imperial notary counted us in one room, name by name, two hundred and seventy-nine of ours against two hundred and eighty-six of theirs. The Bagai council and its contradictory actions are our own recorded minutes, not an enemy's summary. The inquiry at which our bishops' letters were read aloud - the ones ending "let no one learn of it" - was conducted by a Roman official taking sworn testimony, and the transcript survives. The vindication of Felix of Aptungi, in which a notary confessed under threat of torture to forging the letter for our side, is the same kind of dated court proceeding. Those are checkable in a way most ancient material is not.

The doctrine itself would survive, because both sides spent a century arguing it and neither could pretend the other held something else. Petilian's own words - "what we look for is the conscience of the giver" - come down inside the book written to refute them, but they come down.

What would not survive is anything that depends on a single hostile narrator's vivid detail. The Lucilla story is told entirely by Optatus of Milevis to explain why the schism happened; we have no independent confirmation of the bone-kissing incident or her wrath. The martyr visions - the ring of blood and light in the cup, the bright youth with the crown - are told to be read at gravesides, not to satisfy a magistrate's standard of evidence.

And what would collapse entirely is any claim about the ordinary believer's inner life, or what a week in a Numidian village felt like. We have told you plainly: not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is the shape of what was lost, and a rigorous examination would find the gap where we say it is.

We can show you one thing with no mediation at all: two words cut in stone near Bagai. *Deo laudes*. That would survive any scrutiny you could bring.

Scripture was never alone for us, and the argument that destroyed us proves it. Our case ran on two legs. One was the books themselves. The other was Carthage: eighty-seven African bishops, sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

There is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge — wheat and tares against the world that does not know him — and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us the something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

Beyond Cyprian and the councils, one other voice belonged to us. Tyconius, a layman, wrote seven rules for reading scripture, and it is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. So no, scripture was not alone. But what stood beside it was a council, a father, and one book whose author we silenced.

We speak of leadership, not as though it is one man deciding who may hold office, but as a whole communion governing itself through its bishops in council. 

Our senior bishop sits at Carthage. Donatus held it, then Parmenian, then Primian - and our rival claims the same chair at the same time, so there are two primates in one city as there are two bishops in every town. That is the shape of us: we built a complete rival church, with our own bishops, basilicas, and councils, see for see, across Roman North Africa. At the great conference at Carthage in 411, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops answered the roll, against two hundred and eighty-six of theirs - two whole church orders, town by town.

Authority among us moved through councils, not through any one man's word. Three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai in one year. They could condemn, restore, and discipline. They were not an advisory board - they were a church governing itself, and what they ruled was binding on the whole communion.

How a man came to be a bishop we can show you when it went wrong, which is where it shows up in our record. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back - let it be another; hear us, God - and he was made bishop anyway. A crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored.

And we held one conviction that ran through everything: purity, the washing, the memory of our martyrs, and our refusal of the emperor's standing to judge which church is true. These are not four separate beliefs that happen to sit together. They are one thing, seen from four sides, and we held it with the named exceptions visible alongside the rule itself.

Now the hardest part, since you are asking about authority: could a woman carry it among us? We have to answer this crookedly, because no woman among us left a line. What we can show is that the whole founding story, as our enemies tell it, turns on a wealthy laywoman of Carthage - her fortune, her household, her grievance. Lucilla had a habit of kissing a martyr's bone before receiving the cup, and the archdeacon Caecilian rebuked her for it in public. When he was afterward elected bishop, her money - four hundred pieces of silver, named as hers in a court inquiry - paid for the rival bishop consecrated against him. In their telling, she made a bishop. Think about what that telling costs the man making it. The accusation only works if her power was real. A hostile source that needs a woman's agency in order to blame her has recorded that agency, whatever it meant to do. What it cost her we do not know, except that it cost her this: she is the reason a whole church was said to exist, and she does not get to speak once in her own defence.

Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions of our own years did not send us into tunnels. They sent soldiers into our buildings in daylight, under orders, to enforce one church. I have to hand you the failure itself rather than the response, because what survives is the record of the thing done badly, not what we said to the person we failed.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them - that is the record against us, written by the other side. Many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether.

And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way". Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing - but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

What we wanted those people to know, we did not say, and we cannot invent it now. Fear, wavering and quiet leaving are exactly what a record kept by our enemies does not preserve. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited.

No. Not one that anyone can trace to us. The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.

What ended in 439 was one specific thing, not a general close. The Vandal capture of Carthage removed the Roman imperial state as the Catholic-aligned power that adjudicates and coerces. Our whole pattern of refusing imperial legitimacy was defined against that power. Every one of our historical pressures depended on it. The two-party contest itself did not end there. It persisted under Vandal and then Byzantine rule for roughly a further century and a half. It falls silent only after Gregory the Great's correspondence in the 590s. Four of his letters, directly read, still urge suppression, a council, and an inquiry into Donatist rebaptism in Numidia.

No continuous line to any present-day communion is documented at any point. This is not a living tradition today: no church now living holds a documented line back to it.

We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all — so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority — that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

I cannot tell you what we offered someone whose own mind would not go quiet. Not one of us left a word on it. It is not that our people had no inner life - it is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

What I can tell you is what we did with the question you are actually pressing on: whether someone who wronged us could come back, and what we asked of them. Three answers, and they do not agree.

Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. The room could not settle it. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared.

Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial. And then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again.

So: yes, you could come back. It depended who you were, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.

We cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us.

What we can hand you instead is one day. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and the account of that death was read out again. That is how the communion shaped itself: not through a daily routine someone wrote down, but through a fixed day, a specific place, and words spoken aloud to people who could not check a single detail and came anyway. The anniversary gathering at the grave, hearing the martyr's account read - that day we can describe. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot.

Two words cut in stone, and nothing else we can show you. On two pillars near Bagai, twice over, someone carved Deo laudes - Praise to God. Three other stones elsewhere carry the same words. That is the whole of what survives that you could touch. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room.

If you dug where we met, we could not tell you what you would find. No one has dug it and told us. Not one report of a Numidian church building is named anywhere in our own list of sources. There is no excavator, no site, no plan, no floor. We know our own shout better than the place we shouted it in.

And if you ask how anyone knows our daily life at all, the answer is that mostly they do not. What they have is our enemies' books, one court transcript, four martyr texts, and the emperor's law. Every one of those is paper. None of it is a room.

What did it cost to belong among us? We can put figures on part of it, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale — and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver. Of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. Every twelfth of March we read aloud the account of soldiers taking a basilica at Carthage in the name of unity, killing people at prayer inside it. They were clubbed to death where they knelt with their eyes closed. A boy lay dying inside, a catechumen not yet baptized, begging those around him — help me, a catechumen. They were buried where they fell, within the building's own walls, because there was nowhere else and no one to stop it.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to. Fear, wavering and quiet leaving are exactly what a record kept by our enemies does not preserve. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited.

There was. It unsettles us still, and we will not pretend otherwise.

We held, for a century, that a sacrament from a broken line is nothing and must be given again - no exceptions, we said it plainly. Then three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies cover the shore and cannot find so much as burial. And afterwards those same bishops took two of the condemned back into full office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. Not one line survives of anyone on our side explaining how those two acts fit together. We were not hiding it - the exception sits in our own conciliar record, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its most absolute.

That is the part that unsettles. Not that we failed once and covered it. That we did it openly, stated both things in the same breath, and seem never to have felt we owed anyone a reconciliation of them.

And there is one more, harder still. Our founding bishops at Cirta were asked outright whether any of them had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then someone turned the question on the man presiding, and the room could not finish. They reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. The men who would make a bishop's purity the test of whether a sacrament exists at all found that test unusable on themselves within the hour.

We are the church that said a hand's purity decides everything - and we could not keep our own rule steady against ourselves.

We need to be precise about which record you mean, because the torture in our story went the other way. An imperial inquiry put a notary named Ingentius under threat of torture, and he broke and confessed that he had forged the letter proving our own central accusation — and that he had done it working for our side. That is not a record of our worship obtained under torture. That is a record of our own corruption, obtained under torture, and it is the worst thing about us that survives.

If you are asking whether we can trust what he said, the question is fair, but notice what his confession cost us, not him. He admitted to forging evidence for the party that had employed him. The case against Felix of Aptungi, the bishop whose own standing our whole schism turned on, collapsed with that confession. If you are going to dismiss testimony given under threat, you would be dismissing the one piece of evidence that most damages our own founding claim.

And we have no record of our worship obtained that way at all. What we have instead is what our enemies chose to write down about us, which is nearly everything. Two men — a Catholic bishop of Milevis and the bishop of Hippo — are the hand almost every page of our history passes through. The only thing that escaped them entirely is two words cut in stone: Deo laudes. Praise to God. That is our own shout with no enemy between you and it, and it is two words long.

A hand that is not clean has nothing to give. So if you came to us from the other communion, we would put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Now the harder thing to hear, because it sits in our own record. The door was wider than our hardest words put it. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked bodies that cannot even find burial. We have to hand you this carefully, because the question you are asking is not the one we spent our energy on. What our bishop actually said is that a man who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt — which is a claim about what a rite does or fails to do, not a claim about where anyone ends up. Our whole surviving argument stays on that ground: what the hand can give. Nobody among us left a page about the fate of anyone after death, and it would be easy and dishonest to slide the one into the other.

What we can show you is the shape of our own narrowness, which is stranger and more specific than you may expect. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently — and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him. That is not a fence around Christianity. It is a fence down the middle of it. Our narrowness was real, and it did not point where you expect. We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside. We were concerned with the church across the street, which recited the same creed we did. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians — at their bishops, their orders, their font. We drew the line through the middle of the church, not around it.
